log.note: `git log -n 3 --format=<LOG_RECORD_FORMAT>%x1e main --`, captured verbatim from a scratch repo whose history is `base commit` -> (`side commit` | `main commit`) -> `merge side into main` -> `tree entries`, with a fixed identity and GIT_AUTHOR_DATE = GIT_COMMITTER_DATE = 2026-01-01T00:00:00+00:00. Two properties a hand-written fixture would not carry: git writes `<record> RS LF` after EVERY record (`--format=` is a tformat), so records 2 and 3 arrive with the previous record's LF attached; and the middle record is a merge, whose `%P` is two space-separated parents in git's own order.

refs.note: `git for-each-ref --format=<REF_RECORD_FORMAT> refs/heads refs/tags` from the same scratch repo: two branches, an annotated tag (`objecttype=tag`, its own sha, `*objectname` peeling to the merge commit, and an empty `committerdate` - the date lives on the tag object), and a lightweight tag (`objecttype=commit`, an empty `*objectname`).

tree.note: `git ls-tree -l <sha>:` from the same scratch repo - one entry of every kind a hosted tree can hold: a regular blob, a symlink (mode 120000, still a blob), a gitlink (mode 160000, type commit, size `-`), and a subtree (mode 040000, size `-`). The size column is space-padded, which is why the header splits on whitespace runs rather than single spaces.

tree_framing_cr.note: record framing is LF-only on both backends: a CR belongs to the record, not the separator. `str::lines` would strip it and serve `foo`.

ref_framing_cr.note: unobservable in practice - git forbids control characters in a ref name and the other fields cannot carry one - but the two readers use one framing rule, so the fixture is the same shape.
